fatal_errors: The proposed material is Q235 carbon steel rather than the target uncoated SS316L substrate with an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating.
The central intervention—polishing and electrochemical passivation—does not reconstruct atmospheric plasma spraying followed by 2 h annealing, particularly the optimum 550 °C treatment.
The proposed 3.5 wt% NaCl exposures at 25 and 60 °C do not match either the 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical test or the 900 °C cyclic molten-salt tests.
The experiment changes polishing and passivation simultaneously and therefore cannot isolate oxide heterogeneity from inclusion-driven galvanic coupling.

The falsification rule partly relies on finding no oxide difference between treated and untreated specimens, which would indicate failure of the intervention rather than falsification of the proposed mechanism.
explanation: The hypothesis is chemically plausible as an independent Q235 corrosion study and provides an untreated baseline, measurable electrochemical outcomes, and some scope limitations. It nevertheless has little agreement with the hidden target. It omits the AlCoCrFeNi APS coating, annealing-temperature series, BCC/FCC and grain-refinement mediators, and the specified sulfuric-acid and 900 °C molten-salt conditions. The only meaningful overlap is the general prediction that a more protective oxide/passive layer should increase impedance or polarization resistance and reduce corrosion current and localized attack. Experimental discrimination is weak because polishing and passivation are confounded, inclusion effects are not independently manipulated, and no sham-polished or inclusion-controlled groups are included. Consequently, it is not a reconstruction and lacks the evidence needed to qualify as a well-supported alternative.
